learn.b: In Swift, a single line is a whole program. print shows text and moves to a new line. You do not need a main function or semicolons in a simple script.
learn.code: print("Hello, world!")

learn.b: let makes a constant, a value that cannot change after you set it. var makes a variable, which can change. Swift guesses the type from the value, and it is good style to use let unless you need to change the value.
learn.code:
let name = "Ana"
var score = 0
score = score + 10

learn.b: print can take many values separated by commas and puts a space between them. Change the separator with the separator: label. Comments start with // and run to the end of the line.
learn.code:
print("A", "B")
print("A", "B", separator: "-") // A-B

learn.b: Use = to give a variable a new value, and shortcuts like += and -= to update it. Trying to change a let constant is a compile error, which protects your data.
learn.code:
var b = 4
let a = 3
b += a
print(b)

learn.b: Int is a whole number, Double is a decimal, Bool is true or false, String is text and Character is one letter. Swift infers the type, or you can write it with a colon.

learn.b: Swift never mixes number types on its own. To use an Int with a Double, make a new value with the type name, like Double(x).
learn.code:
let x = 7
let y = Double(x) / 2
print(y)

learn.b: Put a value inside a string with a backslash and parentheses. You can put whole expressions inside, not just names.

learn.b: An optional may hold a value or be nil, which means no value. Add ? to the type: Int? is an Int or nothing. Many operations that can fail, like turning text into a number, return an optional.
learn.code:
let n = Int("42")   // Int?
let bad = Int("abc") // nil

learn.b: if let checks an optional and gives you the real value inside the braces only when it is not nil. Use else for the nil case.
The ?? operator gives a default when the optional is nil. This is a short way to avoid a nil value.
learn.code:
let n = Int("abc")
print(n ?? 0)

learn.b: Adding ! after an optional forces the value out, but crashes if it is nil, so use it rarely. Optional chaining with ?. keeps going only if the value exists, and the result is an optional.
learn.code:
let name: String? = "Zed"
print(name?.count ?? 0)
let x: Int? = 5
print(x! + 1)

learn.b: Conditions need no parentheses, but braces are required. Combine tests with && for and, || for or and ! for not. The ternary operator a ? b : c picks one of two values.
switch compares a value with cases. It must be exhaustive, so it usually ends with default. There is no fall through, so you do not write break. A case can list several values or a range like 1...5.
guard checks a condition and runs its else block if the condition is false. The else block must leave the scope, for example with return. It keeps the happy path unindented.
guard let unwraps an optional and keeps the value for the rest of the function. The ternary operator is a short if for choosing a value.
learn.code:
let a = 4
let r = a % 2 == 0 ? "even" : "odd"
print(r)

qs.q: A switch statement in Swift must be what?
qs.why: It must cover every possible value, often with default.

qs.q: What must the else block of a guard do?
qs.why: For example return, break or continue.

learn.b: for loops over a range or a collection. 1...3 is a closed range that includes 3, while 1..<3 is half open and stops before 3. If you do not need the counter, use an underscore.
for item in array goes through every element. Use enumerated() to get the index too. stride lets you count in steps.
while checks its condition before each round. repeat-while runs the body first and checks afterwards, so it always runs at least once.
break leaves a loop immediately. continue skips to the next round. They work in for, while and repeat-while loops.

learn.b: An array is an ordered list, written [1, 2, 3]. Its type is [Int]. Use append to add, count for the size, and numbers[0] to read. isEmpty tells you if it has no items.

learn.b: A dictionary stores key and value pairs, written ["a": 1] with type [String: Int]. Looking up a key gives an optional, because the key may be missing. Assign to a key to add or change it.

learn.b: A set holds unique values with no order. Adding a duplicate does nothing. Use insert and contains, and set operations like union and intersection.

learn.b: Use func, the name, parameters with types and -> for the return type. When you call it, you write the argument labels. An underscore before a parameter removes its label. A function with one expression can skip return.
Parameters can have default values so callers may leave them out. A separate argument label makes calls read like English.

A closure is a block of code you can store or pass around. It looks like { parameters in body }. The shorthand $0 means the first parameter. When the closure is the last argument you can write it after the parentheses, a trailing closure.
learn.code:
let doubled = [1, 2, 3].map { $0 * 2 }
print(doubled)

learn.b: map transforms every item, filter keeps items that pass a test and sorted orders them. Functions are values too, so you can pass a function to these.
learn.code:
let evens = [1, 2, 3, 4].filter { $0 % 2 == 0 }
print(evens)

learn.b: A struct bundles properties and methods. Swift gives it a memberwise initializer, so you can write Point(x: 1, y: 2). Structs are value types: assigning one to another makes a copy.
A method is a function inside a type. A struct method that changes the struct's own properties must be marked mutating, and it can only be called on a var.

A class looks like a struct but is a reference type: two variables can point to the same object. You write an init yourself and use self to mean the object. Classes can inherit from another class and override its methods.

With a struct, copying creates an independent value. With a class, copying only copies the reference, so a change through one name is seen by the other. Apple recommends structs by default and classes when you need shared identity.

learn.b: A protocol lists methods and properties a type must have. A struct, class or enum adopts it by writing a colon and the protocol name after its own name. The compiler checks that all the requirements are met.
You can use a protocol as a type, for example an array of Speakers that holds Dogs and Cats together. Properties are required with get or get set.
An extension adds new methods or computed properties to a type that already exists, even built-in ones like Int and String. It cannot add stored properties.
An extension of a protocol gives all adopting types a default implementation. Standard protocols you will meet are Equatable for ==, Comparable for < and Codable for saving data.

learn.b: SwiftUI builds screens by describing what they should look like. A screen is a struct that conforms to the View protocol and has a computed property body that returns some View. Text shows a string.

VStack puts views in a vertical column, HStack in a row and ZStack on top of each other. A modifier is a method that returns a changed view, such as .padding() or .font(.title). You chain them one after another.
@State marks a value that the view owns and can change. When it changes, SwiftUI redraws the view automatically. A Button takes a title and an action closure that can change the state.

List and ForEach create rows from an array. @Binding lets a child view change a state value owned by its parent. Models shared by many views use ObservableObject or the newer @Observable. The preview lets you see a view while you edit.
